thesis: Per unit of electricity generated, nuclear power causes far fewer deaths and far lower lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions than fossil fuels — comparable to wind and solar — so the objection to nuclear rests on catastrophic tail-risk, waste longevity, cost, and proliferation, not on its ordinary safety or climate record.

positions.name: Comparative-safety consensus (deaths per TWh)
positions.gist: Per unit of electricity, nuclear's death rate is orders of magnitude below coal/oil/gas and on par with wind and solar, driven mainly by fossil-fuel air pollution.

positions.name: Low lifecycle GHG / climate record
positions.gist: Nuclear's lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions (~12 gCO2eq/kWh) are comparable to wind and solar and roughly two orders of magnitude below coal, making it a low-carbon source.

positions.name: Prevented-mortality / decarbonization value
positions.gist: By displacing fossil fuels, historical nuclear generation has prevented on the order of a million air-pollution deaths and tens of gigatonnes of CO2, and can materially aid climate mitigation as firm baseload.

positions.name: Catastrophic tail-risk / normal accidents
positions.gist: The real objection is low-probability, high-consequence catastrophe: nuclear plants are interactively complex and tightly coupled, so severe system accidents (Chernobyl, Fukushima) are inevitable and average death rates understate the tail.

positions.name: Waste longevity & proliferation
positions.gist: Spent fuel and separated plutonium stay hazardous for 100,000+ years and reprocessing spreads weapons-usable material, so long-term stewardship and proliferation—not day-to-day safety—are the core problems.

positions.name: Nuclear economics / cost (LCOE)
positions.gist: New-build nuclear is expensive and slow—LCOE far above wind and solar, with chronic capital cost overruns (e.g. Vogtle)—so cost, not safety, is the decisive strike against it.

positions.name: 100%-renewables feasibility (nuclear unnecessary)
positions.gist: A fully renewable wind-water-solar system can reliably and cheaply power society without nuclear, so nuclear's risks and costs are simply unnecessary to bear.

positions.name: Firm-power / system-cost value of nuclear
positions.gist: Deep decarbonization is much cheaper and less risky when firm low-carbon resources like nuclear complement variable wind and solar; a renewables-only grid faces steeply rising system costs.

benchmark_claims.claim: Death rate per unit of electricity generated, by source (accidents plus air pollution)
benchmark_claims.value: Coal ~24.6, oil ~18.4, gas ~2.8 deaths/TWh; nuclear ~0.03, wind ~0.04, solar ~0.02 deaths/TWh

benchmark_claims.claim: Median lifecycle greenhouse-gas emissions by source (IPCC AR5, 2014)
benchmark_claims.value: Nuclear median 12 gCO2eq/kWh; wind onshore 11; solar PV 48; coal 820; natural gas 490

benchmark_claims.claim: Deaths and CO2 emissions prevented by historical nuclear power (Kharecha & Hansen 2013)
benchmark_claims.value: ~1.84 million air-pollution deaths and ~64 GtCO2-eq prevented (1971-2009)

benchmark_claims.claim: Death tolls of the two worst nuclear accidents (the tail-risk realized)
benchmark_claims.value: Chernobyl: <100 confirmed, best estimate ~300-500 incl. projected cancers; Fukushima: 1 radiation death plus ~2,313 evacuation-related deaths

benchmark_claims.claim: Effect of firm low-carbon resources on deep-decarbonization electricity cost (Sepulveda et al. 2018)
benchmark_claims.value: Including firm low-carbon resources cuts the cost of a zero-carbon grid by 10%-62% across ~1,000 modeled cases

benchmark_claims.claim: Levelized cost of new-build nuclear vs utility-scale solar (Lazard, per Breakthrough)
benchmark_claims.value: New nuclear ~$180/MWh (Vogtle) vs utility solar ~$24-96/MWh; gas CC ~$70; onshore wind ~$50
